newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Rates slip in ex-Hong Kong/Europe air cargo market.
newsitem.headline: Rates slip in ex-Hong Kong/Europe air cargo market.

text.p: The air cargo market between Hong Kong and Europe has slumped into its traditional slack season with both volumes and rates falling, a Reuters survey shows.

After a generally exceptionally busy start to the year for both freight forwarders and airlines - Lufthansa Cargo reported its best four month year start for five years - demand has slumped since the beginning of the month as the industry enters its quietest time of the year.
The question is how long will the slack season last?

Over-capacity has been accompanied by pressure on rates and despite airline cargo managers' determination to maintain peak season rates for as long as possible, freight forwarders said deals are being done and the rate trend is definitely downward.

Lufthansa Cargo - which along with Cathay Pacific Cargo operates the busiest ex Hong Kong European cargo destination to Frankfurt with 11 freighters per week - reported a drop in volume which has created immediate pressure on rates.

Lufthansa Cargo's general manager for Hong Kong, Macau and South China, Frank Berweger was also critical of some airlines, including Cathay, for immediately dropping rates as soon as demand fell in early May. Lufthansa and Cathay operate a separate pricing policy.
"Unfortunately there are some people in this industry who believe if there is no cargo and they drop their rates they will earn more money which I do not understand," Berweger said.

The slump arrived after a remarkable start to the year, Berweger added. That is in line with Lufthansa Cargo overall cutting losses to DM10 million which is a third of what they were a year ago, according to industry observers. However, the group is still expecting losses of around DM40 million for the whole year.

"Hong Kong had an excellent first four months to the year - the best in five years and much, much higher than expected. Volume went up by 10 per cent and yields by even more. To put that into perspective though, last year was a very poor year. Since the beginning of May we have seen a drop in volumes and there is just no demand at the moment which creates immediate pressure on rates.

"The question is how we get through these next two months which is traditionally not very strong. After that if we experience the same sort of boom that we had last year it is going to be a superb year for us," Berweger said.
Freight forwarders also reported a slide in rates and with more competition to sell space deals are more readily available from the airlines.
"Within the past 10 days rates have started to drift down. Before we were paying HK$22-23 per kilo, now we are paying HK$21," said one well known forwarder.

"This is the time of year when freight forwarders like to get big shipments because we can beat down the airlines on price whereas in the peak season we can't. Now the airlines are hungry for cargo and some of them are coming under pressure to cut their rates to get the business. More deals can be now now," the forwarder added.

Another freight forwarder, Freight Express International Ltd (FEI), a subsidiary of MSAS Cargo International (FE) Ltd and specialists in European air cargo, said more customers opt to transport by sea than air at this time of year.

"The air cargo market to Europe is slack and there seems to be excessive airline capacity which is putting considerable pressure on rates. Traditionally people transport goods by sea at this time of year. The question is how prolonged the slack period will be this year. It changes every year but the situation this year is much more bouyant," said an FEI spokesman.
Hong Kong's major airline, Cathay Pacific, agreed the air cargo market to Europe from Hong Kong has softened recently after a "very good" start to the year.
But a Cargo division spokesman said the airline has been able to utilise its feeder network into Hong Kong to allocate more space to other Asian ports requiring capacity to Europe.

"We are able to turn up the volume from some of our ports which feed into Hong Kong and are able to supplement the shortfall. They get more space than they normally would so we are able to keep aircraft reasonably full to Europe. The Europeans have also gone a little quiet on us with traffic into Hong Kong but we are not panicking yet. We are ever hopeful that the slack season will not last long," he said.
Cathay said it is considering reducing capacity over the next few weeks taking advantage of the reduced demand to have essential maintenance carried out on its Boeing 747 cargo aircraft .

Cathay also said the forthcoming holiday to celebrate the territory's handover to China at the end of June may affect traffic levels as importers and exporters avoid what is expected to be a five day long break.
"It is an unusual year this year and that long holiday might be a little glitch when our planes will be awfully empty which we will have to factor into our operations," the spokesman said.
Hong Kong Air Cargo Terminals Ltd (HACTL), said exports have dropped significantly recently as the market suffers its traditional slow down.

HACTL also reported a weaker perishable import pattern this year with air imports of Durian sharply reduced. A HACTL spokesman blamed new methods of stopping the fruit from ripening during transit and bulk transport by sea instead.
Air France Cargo said "things are not too bad." compared to last year's slack season which is generally agreed to have hit the industry hard.

Philippe Bour, regional cargo manager for Air France Cargo in China and Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, said rates had been maintained and load factors were between 70-80 per cent "which was surprising for May." Cargo rates which had fallen to as low as HK$17 per kilo last year had been maintained so far this year at above the HK$20 level, he said.

"Yes, the market is falling and we will have to adapt the rate but I hope we will not go below HK$20. Unlike last year we do not want to increase the rate every few weeks which makes it difficult for the forwarder and their customers. We would like to increase rates in August if the market is there and to increase a second time in October and that will be it" Bour said.

Air France was also temporarily cancelling one of its three weekly freighter flights this week due to three public holidays in France which had temporarily reduced demand for French air exports to Hong Kong.

"I think we can be a bit optimistic about the coming weeks and for sure it will be better than last year. It has been a very nice and surprising start to the year. It seems the export growth from Hong Kong to France has been much higher over the last couple of months than to Germany and the UK. It seems the French economy is recovering and people are spending again and department stores are stocking up," Bour said.

Air France has also increased both pure freighter and passenger capacity on the Paris to Hong Kong route. The carrier's Saturday freighter flight used to share cargo space 60 to 40 per cent in Hong Kong's favour with Osaka in Japan. Now the flight has been re-routed and all 100 tonnes capacity is for Hong Kong customers, Bour said. But Air France is continuing to phase out its Boeing 747 Combi aircraft replacing them with Boeing 747-400 all-passenger aircraft. By the end of June, Air France will operate four Combi and three B747-400 passenger aircraft on its Hong Kong to Paris daily service.

British Airways said the market had fallen into its traditional seasonal trough from the beginning of May which coincided with the labour day holiday in China and heavy rains which had hampered cross border road transport.

Chris Chan, BA World Cargo's area manager for the Greater China region, said a five per cent fall in tonnages had been accompanied by a five per cent rate cut at the start of the month to try and retain volume.
"It is a short term incentive to try and attract business," Chan said.
Despite the slump, substantial quantities of computer peripherals were being air freighted from the Pearl River area in China to Europe on BA's three freighters per week to London, Chan added.

From May 17, British Airways is switching its Hong Kong cargo flights from Gatwick to Stansted which the airline said is more cargo friendly and will free up passenger slots at London's second airport. The airline also plans to increase its wet leased freighter operation between the UK and Hong Kong to five times weekly by wet leasing a second aircraft for the route later this year.
BA is just one airline which is increasing cargo capacity between Hong Kong and Europe.

Air China recently began a Beijing to London Boeing 747 Combi service via Hong Kong. Initially a once weekly service, China's flag carrier is expected to increase the schedule after Hong Kong is handed back to Chinese rule. Industry observers said Air China's cargo rates had been sharply reduced to try and win business.

Taiwan's EVA Air, part of Taiwan's Evergreen Group, which includes Evergreen Marine, the world's biggest container shipping company, has also expanded its European services. This month, EVA started a three times weekly passenger flight from Taipei to Amsterdam via Dubai. A twice weekly freighter service from Taipei to Brussels via Singapore and Dubai also began on May 9 using a McDonnell Douglas MD-11 freighter with around 80 tonnes cargo capacity supplementing a once weekly cargo flight to Amsterdam.

Another growing presence in the Hong Kong to Europe cargo market is Emirates Airline. It will double cargo capacity between Hong Kong and its Dubai hub when it introduces new Boeing 777 aircraft to the route from October 1, the airline's Hong Kong cargo manager Jacky Lau said.
Industry observers said the general rise in cargo capacity is expected to coincide with renewed pressure on ex Hong Kong cargo rates later this year.
